:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x, y) =3x^2+4xy$ at the point $A(0,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,4).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇g(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we found that the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ is

$$
∇\,f(1,1)=∇(\text{div}\,V)\,{|}_{(1,\,1)}=4\,i+2\,j.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(4\,i+2\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{5}(-3\,i+4\,j)) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 4}{5} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=\sqrt{3}\,i+j.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+{1}^{2}}=2 \\ u & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy)\text{ }j \\  & =y\,i+x\,j \\ ∇\,f(2,1) & =i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(2,1) & =∇\,f(2,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+2\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{1(\sqrt{3})+2(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ at the point $(0,-1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=3\,i+4\,j.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}j \\ ∇\,f(0,-1) & =\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-1)}{{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,-1) & =∇\,f(0,-1)\cdot u \\  & =-2\,j\cdot \frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-\frac{2(4)}{5} \\  & =-\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i-j.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)-1)\,i+(2(1)-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j) \\  & =\frac{1(1)+1(-1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y$ at the point $A(1,0)$ in the direction towards the point $B(0,1).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,1⟩-⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(1,0) & =⟨{e}^{0}+2\cdot 1\cdot 0,\,1\cdot {e}^{0}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,0) & =∇f(1,0)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ at the point $(0,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=3i+5j.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}=\sqrt{34} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{34}}(3i+5j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2y)\text{ }j \\  & =12x\,i+2\,j \\ ∇\,f(0,1) & =(12\cdot 0)\,i+2\,j \\  & =2j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇\,f(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =2j\cdot (\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}i+\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}j) \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 3+2\cdot 5}{\sqrt{34}} \\  & =\frac{10\sqrt{34}}{34}.\end{aligned}
$$
